groups.title: Web Foundations Theory
groups.question: A client wants a fast, secure marketing site with a blog and a contact form, and asks why you suggest a JAMstack site instead of a classic server-rendered one. Explain the rendering models, the JAMstack idea and why your HTML structure matters.

followUps.Semantic HTML elements and accessibility: Why do semantic elements like article and nav matter for users and search engines?
followUps.Static versus dynamic site rendering mod: What is the difference between serving static HTML and generating it per request?
followUps.JAMstack philosophy and the decoupled ar: What does decoupling the frontend from the backend give a JAMstack site?

evidence.text: Semantic elements describe what each part of the page is.
Screen readers use that meaning to let users jump between regions.
Search engines also use the structure to understand the content.

notEnough: Only saying semantic HTML is best practice.

evidence.text: A static site serves HTML that was built ahead of time, with no server work per request.
A dynamic site builds HTML on each request, which adds work and latency.
Dynamic rendering allows personalised, always-fresh content that static pages cannot easily show.
Pages are pre-built as markup and served from a CDN.
Dynamic features use APIs and serverless functions instead of a server rendering every page.
Less server code exposed means a smaller attack surface and easier scaling.

notEnough: Only spelling out JavaScript, APIs and Markup.

groups.title: CDNs and Edge Delivery Concepts
groups.question: Your static site loads fast in Europe but slowly in Asia, and it shows live weather from a third-party API. Explain how CDNs deliver the site and how the browser gets the live data.

followUps.How content delivery networks cache and: Why does a CDN make a site faster for users far away from your origin server?
followUps.Working with third-party REST APIs in th: How does a static page fetch live data from an API in the browser?

evidence.text: A CDN keeps copies of your files on servers around the world.
Users are served from the nearest copy, so data travels a shorter distance.
That reduces the time to the first byte and load on the origin.
The page uses fetch at runtime to request data from the API.
The response is usually JSON that the code parses and renders.
async/await keeps the code readable, and errors and loading states must be handled.

notEnough: Only saying you call the API.

groups.title: HTML and CSS Tooling
groups.question: You are building the layout of your static site: a header, a three-column card grid that collapses on phones and readable text on every screen. Explain the CSS you would use.

followUps.CSS Flexbox and Grid layout systems hand: When would you use flexbox and when grid?
followUps.Responsive design with media queries and: How do media queries and fluid units make the layout responsive?

evidence.text: Flexbox lays items out in one direction, like a row of header links.
Grid handles rows and columns together, like a card grid.
Both replace older float-based layout tricks.

notEnough: Only saying one is 1D and one is 2D.

evidence.text: Media queries apply different styles at different screen widths.
Relative units like rem, percentages and viewport units scale with the screen or user settings.
Fluid sizing reduces how many breakpoints you need.

notEnough: Only saying you use media queries.

groups.title: JavaScript Essentials Practice
groups.question: Your site's JavaScript calls an API and something is wrong with the data shown. Explain the modern JavaScript you would write and how you would debug it in the browser.

followUps.ES6 features: arrow functions, destructu: Which modern JavaScript features do you use most in framework code and why?
followUps.Browser DevTools for debugging and netwo: How would you use DevTools to check whether an API call returned the right data?

evidence.text: Arrow functions give short function syntax and keep the surrounding this.
Destructuring pulls fields out of objects and arrays in one step.
ES modules split code into files with explicit imports and exports.
The Network tab shows each request with its status and response body.
The console and debugger let you inspect values and step through code.
The Elements panel shows whether the DOM matches what you expected.
